title: What street-level imagery can and cannot tell us about campus sustainability: a measurement study of 252 U.S. campuses
summary: A measurement study links street-level and aerial imagery to 252 U.S. campuses and tests what visible conditions can reveal about sustainability ratings. Imagery captures features such as vegetation but explains only a limited share of institutional sustainability scores.
question: What can campus imagery credibly measure about sustainability?
findings: Imagery explained at most about 10% of variation in STARS overall scores across evaluated models.
Vegetation measurements aligned across street-level and aerial imagery, with substantial seasonality.
The proposed Visible Campus Environment Index describes visible conditions rather than institutional sustainability performance.
sourceBasis: Supplied manuscript dated 30 October 2026; full text reviewed, including discussion and limitations. CV hyperlink for this title is misassigned and is not used. SSRN ID and abstract link independently confirmed in the complete author listing inspected in-browser on 23 November 2026; this does not imply a newly retrieved SSRN full text.

title: Resurrecting Theology: When Historical Scholars Confront the Modern World Through AI
summary: Six language models answer survey questions in the personas of 23 religious and intellectual figures. The study compares responses with and without retrieved texts and finds that model identity accounts for more variation than tradition and scholar combined.
question: Whose views does an AI-generated historical persona express?
findings: The study records 528,375 responses across six language models.
In the main WVS retrieval panel, model identity accounts for 37% of item-level variance, versus 17% for tradition and scholar together.
Retrieval separates personas but does not improve the tested historical contrasts.
sourceBasis: Supplied November 2026 manuscript; abstract and full text reviewed by the PDF review agent. Supplied manuscript takes precedence over older conference descriptions.

title: The Address of the Party: Measuring Partisan Visibility in Turkey
summary: A directory of party organizations and annotated Street View panoramas is used to study where Turkish parties locate offices and display symbols. Offices cluster near commerce, government institutions, and rival parties; nearby symbol shares do not predict changes in electoral support.
question: Where do parties organize, and what do they make visible nearby?
findings: The study examines 5,928 party organizations across 973 districts and 6,496 annotated panoramas.
In the directory, 72% of offices have a rival within 250 meters, compared with 30% under the comparison model.
The paper finds no evidence that symbol shares predict changes in electoral support.
sourceBasis: Supplied November 2026 manuscript; abstract and full-text review by the PDF review agent.

title: Who Speaks at the Court? Bench Roles, Language, and Judicial Voice at the European Court of Human Rights
summary: Recordings of 252 Grand Chamber hearings reveal substantial differences in judges’ participation in public questioning. National judges of respondent states ask questions more often, and documented language proficiency is also associated with participation.
question: Which judges take the floor when every judge has an equal vote?
findings: The data cover 140 judges, 4,254 sittings, and 2,106 question units.
On the same bench, the respondent state’s national judge is 23.1 percentage points more likely to ask a question.
The estimated gender difference is small and imprecise.
sourceBasis: Supplied manuscript dated 22 November 2026; full-text review includes discussion and observational limitations. Kept distinct from Do Judges Have Emotions?, which has a different title and SSRN identifier. SSRN ID and abstract link independently confirmed in the complete author listing inspected in-browser on 23 November 2026; this does not imply a newly retrieved SSRN full text.

title: LUMOS: LLM-based Universal Measure of Salience
venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on Large Language Models (LLM 2026), Springer Nature
summary: LUMOS tests whether multimodal language models can locate the salient object in an image. Asking for a bounding box works much better than asking for a polygon, and a separate segmentation model can sharpen a good localization; specialized saliency models still perform better in the reported benchmark.
question: How much does the way we ask a model to point change what it finds?
findings: The prompt-format comparison reports mean intersection-over-union of 31.1% for polygons and 56.6% for boxes.
Qwen2.5-VL improves from 55.8% overlap with box prompting to 88.6% after Segment Anything mask refinement; the three specialized saliency baselines reach 96.6–97.8% under the paper’s protocol.
Refinement helps models that place useful boxes; it gives little benefit when the initial localization is wrong.

Unparsable responses are excluded from metric calculations, and evaluated sample counts differ by model. The benchmark measures overlap with salient-object annotations, rather than direct eye-tracking attention.
sourceBasis: Full SSRN manuscript downloaded through the ordinary authorized browser UI on 23 November 2026 and reviewed locally, including methods, results, discussion, and relevant appendices. 28-page manuscript dated 24 February 2026. Main results and valid-output denominators in Tables 3–4 (PDF p6), prompt parsing/exclusion rules p4, discussion pp6–7, qualitative examples pp10–24, toolkit and usage appendix pp25–28. Forthcoming proceedings status remains from the latest CV.

stories.title: Asking for a box changes the result
stories.sourceBasis: Full downloaded LUMOS manuscript: prompt comparison, parsing rules, Tables 3–4, and Figure 3.
paragraphs: A bird in flight is an easy image for a person to recognize. Asking a multimodal model to mark its important region is a more demanding task: the answer must also take a usable spatial form. LUMOS compares those answers directly. In the prompt-format test, requesting boxes rather than a long list of polygon vertices raises mean overlap from 31.1% to 56.6%. A segmentation model can then recover a much better outline when the box is useful. The original figure makes the failure modes visible: different models can describe the same image yet point to different regions. Failed-to-parse answers are excluded from the reported scores, so reliability includes more than the overlap statistic alone.

title: Victim Assistance Using Large Language Models: The Case of a Massive Earthquake in Hatay, Turkey
venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on the AI Revolution: Research, Ethics, and Society (AIR-RES 2026), Springer Nature
summary: An experiment uses ten language models to simulate sentiment responses of hypothetical Hatay residents to earthquake-related events. Responses vary with persona characteristics and model choice, illustrating the scale of synthetic survey research and the need for validation against survivors’ experiences.
question: How do language models simulate disaster-related sentiment across demographic personas, and how consistent are those simulations across models?
findings: The experiment generates 146,880 synthetic observations from 864 persona types, 17 event scenarios, and ten language models.

Generated sentiment generally improves for aid and volunteer scenarios and declines for floods and disease outbreaks, while elections and government-response scenarios produce model-dependent results.
Model choice changes the magnitude and sometimes the direction of demographic associations. These synthetic responses do not establish actual survivors’ sentiment.
sourceBasis: Local 49-page manuscript dated 23 February 2025, SSRN 5415614; methods, results, tables, conclusion, and appendix figures reviewed. Observations are generated for hypothetical personas, not collected from survivors. The newer CV’s forthcoming publication status is preserved; subgroup directions that differ between abstract and body are not repeated.

title: ACROSS: Accessible Country-Relevant Outlier Selection System
summary: ACROSS combines five outlier-detection and scaling strategies to find unusual country-level observations. On a benchmark built from political-science case studies, it recovers more known outliers than the tested individual methods or Cook’s distance, while also suggesting new cases for closer substantive investigation.
question: Which unusual countries do familiar statistical diagnostics miss?
findings: The comparison evaluates 33 algorithms and 163 method–normalization pairs against 14 literature-derived outlier-detection tasks.
The final ensemble flags an observation when at least one of five selected method–normalization pairs flags it; mean recall is about 0.54, versus about 0.15 for the Cook’s distance baseline.
Normalization changes performance substantially: robust scaling raises CBLOF’s reported improvement over Cook’s distance from about 32% to about 87%.

The known-outlier labels are incomplete and the empirical tasks use one to three dimensions. Additional flagged observations are research leads, and broader generalization requires further validation.
sourceBasis: Full SSRN manuscript downloaded through the ordinary authorized browser UI on 23 November 2026 and reviewed locally, including methods, results, discussion, and relevant appendices. 51-page manuscript dated 28 December 2024. Benchmark construction pp8–15; incomplete-label caveat p15; sensitivity analysis pp16–17; new candidate outliers pp18–20; final maximum-vote ensemble pp20–22; comparison Table 4 p22; appendix tables and code pp32–51. Forthcoming journal status remains from the CV. The 14 tasks include two U.S. cases and should not be marketed as 14 unique countries.

stories.title: A flagged country can be the next case study
stories.sourceBasis: Full downloaded ACROSS manuscript, especially incomplete-label caveat p15, additional cases pp18–20, and ensemble comparison pp21–22.
paragraphs: An unusual observation can challenge a theory or reveal a case worth studying. ACROSS starts with country-level exceptions already discussed in political-science research, then compares how well different algorithms find them. Its five-part ensemble recovers about 54% of the known outlier observations, compared with about 15% for Cook’s distance. It also flags cases outside the original labels, including Haiti’s unusually low military spending and sharp economic changes in post-conflict countries. Those flags are invitations to investigate. The labels do not enumerate every true outlier, and being flagged does not by itself justify deleting an observation or explain why it is unusual.

title: Using Generative AI to Calculate Party Positions: A Comparison of Human Experts and Large Language Models
venue: Journal of Political Institutions and Political Economy
summary: Five language models code 140,432 manifesto segments from Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States. Their estimated left–right positions track the human benchmark but generally compress the ideological range toward the center.
question: Can a model track party positions accurately while still making parties look more moderate?
findings: The July 2024 manuscript compares 84 manifestos containing 140,432 segments, using the same detailed Manifesto Project coding scheme for humans and models.
ChatGPT 3.5 has the highest reported correlation with the human RILE index (0.86) and the lowest reported RMSE (11.83) among the five models tested.
The scatterplot shows flatter fitted relationships than the identity line: left- and right-leaning manifestos are generally estimated less extremely than the benchmark.
The authors identify cases where human and model segment codes both have plausible interpretations; disagreement alone does not prove that the model is wrong.
sourceBasis: Complete 53-page SSRN manuscript dated 26 July 2024 downloaded through the normal SSRN flow and reviewed, including coding prompt, model setup, 84-manifesto results and supplementary country/party comparisons. This is the same dated manuscript linked by USC, not a verified final published PDF; original published status and final catalog author order are retained. Source Figure 3 is explicitly labeled as this manuscript version. The 34 MiB SSRN PDF remains outside the deployment; use the authoritative USC full-text URL.

stories.title: A high correlation can hide systematic moderation
stories.summary: A model can rank manifestos reasonably well while compressing the differences between them.
paragraphs: The authors give five language models the Manifesto Project’s coding scheme, classify individual text segments, and aggregate those labels into left–right scores. In this July 2024 manuscript, ChatGPT 3.5 produces a correlation of 0.86 with the human benchmark.

The scatterplot shows why that correlation is only part of the story. The colored fitted lines are flatter than the dashed identity line: differences between parties are compressed, and more extreme manifestos tend to appear more moderate.

The benchmark also needs judgment. Some segments can reasonably receive more than one code, and isolated sentences can lose context. The study therefore asks whether automation can substitute for expert interpretation, rather than treating every disagreement as a simple model error.
limitations: This figure and its numerical results come from the July 2024 manuscript, not a verified final published PDF.
The comparison tests five particular 2024 model deployments and one prompting setup in three countries.
Human coding is a benchmark with ambiguity; high correlation is not perfect agreement or proof of validity.

title: Measuring political polarization through visible interactions between religious and non-religious citizens
summary: Street videos from Turkey are used to estimate relative distances between pedestrians with different visible gender and religious-attire categories. Same-group pairs, especially women classified as religious, tend to be closer; the published article explicitly distinguishes these spatial patterns from proof of political hostility.
question: When do visible social boundaries also appear in the distances between people?
findings: The study samples 178,413 frames from 1,439 publicly available street videos; its manually annotated training corpus contains 7,450 frames and more than 27,000 labeled people.
The main four-category detector reports mAP50 of 0.581; combining categories improves performance relative to the more detailed eight-category model.
Pairs classified as religious women have consistently smaller normalized distances than the cross-group reference in the main specifications.
The final article states that social distance, homophily and polarization are related but distinct: physical spacing alone does not establish hostility or ideological extremity.
sourceBasis: Final 32-page Scientific Reports version of record downloaded and reviewed, including classification validation, distance normalization, main estimates and the expanded conceptual-clarification/limitations sections. Figures come from this final published version, not the 55-page July 2024 SSRN preprint. Publication status and verified final author order are preserved. Relative distance units are not calibrated meters; attire categories are visual proxies rather than verified beliefs.

stories.title: Closer together does not automatically mean more polarized
stories.summary: The final article treats street-level proximity as evidence of social separation, with several possible explanations.
paragraphs: The study turns public street videos into detected people, visible attire categories and normalized pairwise distances. The clearest same-group closeness appears among people classified as religious women.

The final published article adds an important distinction: social distance, homophily and polarization are not interchangeable. Friends walking together, shared routines, gender norms and the built environment can all produce spatial clustering without hostility toward another group.

The figures expose both parts of the measurement process: estimating depth from a flat image, then comparing relative distances across category pairs. Neither step reads someone’s beliefs or provides a calibrated distance in meters.
limitations: Attire is a visible cue, not a verified statement of religious belief or political identity.
Relative spacing cannot identify animosity or distinguish friendship from chance proximity.
Classification errors, video selection and unobserved relationships affect interpretation.

title: Stochastic Gradient Descent-based Inference for Dynamic Network Models with Attractors
venue: Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics
summary: A stochastic gradient descent approach makes coevolving latent space network models more scalable and allows actors to join or leave over time. Simulations and an application to congressional social-media networks illustrate the method.
question: How can dynamic network models scale while tracking changing membership?
findings: Simulations show improved scalability with little loss of accuracy relative to the compared MCMC estimation.
sourceBasis: Full published article on coauthor website downloaded and reviewed; publisher DOI and 2025 year match CV.

title: Threat Vocalisations are Acoustically Similar between Humans (Homo sapiens) and Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes)
summary: The study compares human and chimpanzee vocalizations across ten equivalent behavioral contexts using acoustic distance and separability measures.
findings: Threat vocalizations are acoustically distinctive from other contexts and similar across the two species.
sourceBasis: Full published article downloaded from the University of Amsterdam repository and reviewed, including discussion and limitations.

title: Disentangling positive and negative partisanship in social media interactions using a coevolving latent space network with attractors model
venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series A
summary: A coevolving latent space model separates attraction within parties from repulsion across parties in Twitter and Reddit networks. The application explores how the balance of these forces changes over time.
question: How do in-group attraction and out-group repulsion shape partisan networks?
sourceBasis: Full author-hosted manuscript reviewed at https://dinopc.org/papers/coevolvinglatent.pdf; arXiv and publisher establish author order, which differs from the CV listing. Findings depend in part on network construction.

title: Varieties of corona news: a cross-national study on the foundations of online misinformation production during the COVID-19 pandemic
summary: A cross-national analysis compares topics and wording in 10,131 fact-checked COVID-19 falsehoods from 129 countries. Some country groups share more similar content, especially those with serious press-freedom problems or low human development, while conspiracy-related themes cross national boundaries.
question: Which parts of pandemic misinformation travel globally, and which vary across countries?
findings: The published study covers January 2020–February 2021 and compares countries using 14 social, economic, political and informational variables.
Topics often appear together: the source heatmap reports 2.165 topics per falsehood on average, with up to eight in one observation.
Content is especially similar within the groups with very serious press-freedom problems and low human development; national characteristics offer limited overall predictive support.
Conspiracies are among the least useful topics for distinguishing country groups. The word-group unusualness measure does not differ significantly across the compared groups.
sourceBasis: Full final Springer article reviewed, including topic coding, similarity measures, country comparisons and discussion. All source figures use the published version (online 13 December 2022; print 2023), rather than the earlier 60-page SSRN submission. Country attribution is from fact-check records and does not establish the true origin of an item; observational comparisons do not identify causal effects of censorship, official announcements or national traits.

stories.title: Shared narratives cross borders, while some content clusters locally
stories.summary: The paper finds a mix of global commonalities and country-group similarities in pandemic misinformation.
paragraphs: A false claim can contain several topics at once. The first figure counts those overlaps: a story can connect a public figure, a purported cure and a claim about government in the same item. The source reports just over two topics per falsehood on average.

The country comparisons show that content from countries with very serious press-freedom problems is often more similar within that group. Yet many national characteristics have limited predictive value, and conspiracies are among the topics least able to distinguish country groups.

The wording also points to common ground: the paper finds no statistically significant differences between country groups in its unusual-word-group measure. These patterns motivate both local communication strategies and attention to narratives that circulate internationally.
limitations: Fact-check records are a selected corpus rather than a census of every falsehood or every person exposed.
An item’s attributed country is not necessarily its original source.
Text similarity does not establish transmission, readership, belief or a causal effect of country characteristics.

title: How does “A Bit of Everything American” state feel about COVID-19? A quantitative Twitter analysis of the pandemic in Ohio
summary: More than 46 million tweets from over 91,000 users in Ohio are used to trace pandemic-related attention, sentiment and emotion. The study compares these county-level measures with COVID-19 cases and deaths during the first four months of 2020.
question: How did the subjects of public conversation change as the pandemic reached Ohio?
findings: The dataset covers all 88 Ohio counties from 1 January to 30 April 2020.
The topic-awareness series rises sharply around March as pandemic discussion becomes more prominent; its policy markers show timing rather than measured policy effects.
Associations between partisan-topic measures and pandemic outcomes differ between the pre-first-case and post-stay-at-home periods. These are county-level relationships.
sourceBasis: Full final Springer article reviewed, including the word-embedding awareness measure, emotion-classification model, pooled OLS and System-GMM specifications, descriptive figures and stated operationalization limits. Source Figure 8 is from the version of record (online April 2021; print 2022). County-level associations cannot establish individual attitudes or causal effects of political identity or public-health policy.

stories.title: Public attention changed as the pandemic reached Ohio
stories.summary: The daily series separates changes in what people discussed from claims about why those changes occurred.
paragraphs: The study gathers tweets from users across Ohio’s 88 counties and follows the first four months of 2020. It uses similarity to topic vocabularies to construct an awareness measure, alongside sentiment and emotion estimates.

The daily visualization shows a sharp increase in illness-related attention around March, with substantial pandemic discussion already occurring before Ohio’s first confirmed case. Vertical lines identify cases and policy dates so the reader can compare their timing.

The paper then analyzes county-level associations with cases and deaths. Those associations change across periods, which makes a static story about political attitudes and pandemic outcomes inadequate. The figure itself remains descriptive: the lines do not demonstrate a policy effect.
limitations: Twitter users and their expressed posts do not represent every Ohio resident.
Awareness, sentiment and emotion are computational proxies rather than direct psychological measurements.
County-level patterns do not reveal an individual’s behavior or establish causality.

title: The Influence of Elite Networks on Green Policy Making
summary: The article combines ministers’ Twitter networks in 34 countries with interviews across seven Northern European countries to examine green-policy outcomes. Stronger connections across elite communities are associated with higher renewable-energy consumption and lower per-capita carbon emissions.
question: Do connections across professional and political circles matter for green policy?
findings: Cross-country models compare ministers’ wider follow networks and ministers-only networks with renewable-energy shares and per-capita CO₂ emissions.
In the wider networks, lower modularity and stronger links across communities are associated with higher renewable-energy consumption and lower emissions; uncertainty varies across specifications.
The qualitative component includes 37 interviews across Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Iceland, Ireland, Belgium and the Netherlands.
Interviews describe more informal cross-sector contact in several higher-performing Nordic cases; the Netherlands is an exception to a simple two-group comparison.
sourceBasis: Complete final Wiley main article and Appendix A read through the ordinary browser’s University of Rochester Library full-access session, including hypotheses, data, methods, all regression tables, fieldwork and conclusions. This is the final Politics & Policy 48(6), 1104–1137 article, not the earlier dissertation chapter. Full text is linked at the publisher and is not rehosted. Follow networks proxy policy relationships; country comparisons, unequal Twitter participation and averaged outcomes do not establish causal influence.

stories.title: The wider circle matters
stories.summary: Looking beyond links among ministers brings professional and social bridges into the policy picture.
paragraphs: A network made only of ministers misses many people who participate in policy discussions. The article therefore studies both ministers’ links to one another and their wider follow networks, using community structure to ask how much those circles connect.

The cross-country results associate stronger bridges and less isolated communities with higher renewable-energy shares and lower per-capita CO₂ emissions. These are associations in country comparisons, not a measured effect of adding a particular contact.

Thirty-seven interviews across seven countries add detail about how such connections work. Several Nordic cases feature informal contact, stable bureaucracies and careers that move across sectors. The Netherlands complicates a simple divide between higher- and lower-performing country groups.
limitations: A Twitter follow is a proxy for a policy relationship, and Twitter participation varies sharply by country.
Cross-sectional network measures and averaged energy outcomes leave substantial scope for confounding and reverse causality.
The seven-country fieldwork helps interpret relationships but is not a representative causal test.

title: Do Judges Have Emotions? What AI Sees at the European Court of Human Rights
summary: Can AI read a judge’s reactions from a courtroom video? We link European Court of Human Rights webcasts to judges, speakers, and judgments. An apparent difference between responses to applicants and governments largely disappears after accounting for where judges turn their heads—a lesson in measuring facial displays without mistaking them for feelings.
question: What can automated measures of facial expression reveal about judges’ courtroom behavior—and how much of the apparent signal comes from the camera?
findings: Across 311 processed recordings, the pipeline produces 372,395 verified judge-seconds. Listening-time coverage is sparse: a verified judge is visible during only 1.4% of the seconds in which a party speaks, and the three most visible judges account for 89% of listening observations.

The classifier initially assigns 3.5 percentage points more negative display during government turns than applicant turns. Accounting for head orientation reduces this to roughly 0.5–0.9 points, with intervals including zero; the raw difference largely reflects which direction judges face.

The study finds no reliable national, regional, or political-affinity differences in listening displays, but camera coverage leaves low power to detect modest effects. The null results do not establish an absence of judicial favoritism.

Facial-display measures do not improve held-out prediction of votes. Stable differences between individual faces, including demographic patterns, may reflect classifier behavior as well as expression and should not be read as judges’ inner emotions.
sourceBasis: Complete 87-page public SSRN PDF (ssrn-7712078.pdf), including all 16 hypotheses, the 311-recording data pipeline, sampling restrictions, pose analyses, specification curves, prediction tests, discussion, and appendices. Public title-page author order is Ezgi Siir Kibris followed by Cantay Caliskan. This public version supersedes the older local 11-hypothesis draft. PDF page numbers are one greater than printed body-page numbers after the title page.
limitations: The outcomes are expression-classifier probabilities, not observed feelings, attitudes, or psychological states. Demographic differences cannot be separated from bias in how the classifier reads faces.
Camera placement and selective coverage strongly constrain inference. National judges appear during both parties’ turns in only 31 hearings.
Head-orientation adjustments are exploratory; human ratings of the same faces and independent replications are needed to distinguish remaining expression signals from measurement artifacts.

stories.title: When a camera angle looks like an emotion
stories.sourceBasis: Public SSRN 7712078 full text, primary party comparison and exploratory head-orientation analyses. The raw negative-display gap is 3.5 percentage points; full-landmark adjustments leave 0.5–0.9 points with intervals including zero.
paragraphs: The first result looked unusually solid: the model read more negativity from judges while governments spoke, and the difference survived 13 specifications. Then we checked where the judges were looking. Applicants and governments sit in different directions, and the classifier tends to call a turned face more neutral. Controlling for head orientation removes most of the apparent party difference. Repeating an analysis many ways cannot repair a measurement flaw shared by all of them.
limitations: The outcomes are expression-classifier probabilities, not observed feelings, attitudes, or psychological states. Demographic differences cannot be separated from bias in how the classifier reads faces.
Camera placement and selective coverage strongly constrain inference. National judges appear during both parties’ turns in only 31 hearings.
Head-orientation adjustments are exploratory; human ratings of the same faces and independent replications are needed to distinguish remaining expression signals from measurement artifacts.

stories.title: The courtroom the camera lets us see
stories.sourceBasis: Public SSRN 7712078 full text; verified listening-sample coverage, role concentration and power discussion. Expression probabilities are model outputs rather than direct measures of emotion.
paragraphs: Hundreds of hours of public hearings yield surprisingly little footage of judges listening. A verified judge is visible during only 1.4% of party-speaking seconds, and three prominently seated judges account for 89% of the listening observations. That uneven view is part of the evidence, not just a technical inconvenience: it limits what we can infer about national favoritism or the behavior of the full bench.
limitations: The outcomes are expression-classifier probabilities, not observed feelings, attitudes, or psychological states. Demographic differences cannot be separated from bias in how the classifier reads faces.
Camera placement and selective coverage strongly constrain inference. National judges appear during both parties’ turns in only 31 hearings.
Head-orientation adjustments are exploratory; human ratings of the same faces and independent replications are needed to distinguish remaining expression signals from measurement artifacts.

title: Legopolitics: Toying with the Enemy — Ludic Framing in Pro-Iranian Wartime Propaganda
summary: How does war propaganda change when it looks like a toy? We study 363 pro-Iranian LEGO-style videos, tracing who gets agency, who receives blame, and whose suffering is shown. The playful format combines selective depictions of violence with references to an adversary’s own politics and popular culture.
question: How do LEGO-style wartime videos distribute agency, blame, and suffering, and how does their language differ from Iranian state media?
findings: Iranian actors occupy the agent role in 65.6% of 1,045 directed confrontations. Of 691 blame attributions directed at either named U.S. leaders or the public, 93.1% target leaders, overwhelmingly Trump; excluding Trump leaves an imprecise 52.5% share, no longer distinguishable from parity.

Within the same video and comparable target types, Iranian-inflicted violence is depicted with 0.77 standard deviations less victim suffering. This measures what the animations show, rather than real-world casualties or audience responses.

Humor is associated with views across channels, but there is no reliable association among comparable videos within the same channel. The study does not establish that humor causes circulation or persuasion.

Video text contains more U.S. domestic-political and popular-cultural references than the state-media comparison, an adjusted difference of 9.7 percentage points. Sacred legitimation is not uniformly reduced: it is especially prominent in the regime-linked core.
sourceBasis: Complete 65-page public SSRN PDF (ssrn-7667619.pdf), including methods, all hypothesis tests, robustness tables, discussion, and appendices. Primary sample: 363 war-period videos, 7,288 scenes and 96,530 sampled frames; five historical reference videos excluded from the main sample. Source pages below use 1-based PDF pages. Figures depicting LEGO-style videos contain AI-generated study material, not website design illustrations.
limitations: Interpretive scene labels come from an LLM. Independent computer-vision checks validate some concrete objects more successfully than subjective narrative judgments such as suffering or responsibility.
The discoverable-video sample omits deleted and less visible material; provenance categories do not establish direct state control.
The five-outlet state-media baseline is temporally unmatched, and engagement totals are collection-time snapshots rather than causal measures of audience effects.

stories.title: Who gets to suffer in a toy war?
stories.sourceBasis: Public SSRN 7667619 full text; H2a/H2c main and robustness results. The stills are explicitly AI-generated LEGO-style propaganda analyzed as study material.
paragraphs: The playful surface does political work. Across 363 LEGO-style wartime videos, violence attributed to Iran is shown with substantially less victim suffering than adversary violence, even within the same video and comparable target types. Yet the story is not simply that jokes travel farther: once we compare posts from the same channel, humor has no reliable relationship with views. These are patterns in the representation and circulation of propaganda, not evidence of its effects on viewers.
limitations: Interpretive scene labels come from an LLM. Independent computer-vision checks validate some concrete objects more successfully than subjective narrative judgments such as suffering or responsibility.
The discoverable-video sample omits deleted and less visible material; provenance categories do not establish direct state control.
The five-outlet state-media baseline is temporally unmatched, and engagement totals are collection-time snapshots rather than causal measures of audience effects.

stories.title: Blaming a president, addressing a public
stories.sourceBasis: Public SSRN 7667619 full text, H1b and H3b. Comparison media are temporally unmatched and cannot establish producer strategy or audience effects.
paragraphs: In the videos’ direct leader-versus-public blame attributions, 93.1% name a U.S. leader. Almost all of that personalization concerns Trump; remove him and the remaining leaders receive about as much blame as the American public. The videos also draw on U.S. taxes, prices, political scandals, and popular culture more than the state-media comparison does. The combination illustrates how hostile messaging can borrow the language of the audience it hopes to address.
limitations: Interpretive scene labels come from an LLM. Independent computer-vision checks validate some concrete objects more successfully than subjective narrative judgments such as suffering or responsibility.
The discoverable-video sample omits deleted and less visible material; provenance categories do not establish direct state control.
The five-outlet state-media baseline is temporally unmatched, and engagement totals are collection-time snapshots rather than causal measures of audience effects.

title: Measuring the Playable Past: Evaluating Architectural Accuracy in Assassin’s Creed, Age of Empires, and Battlefield
summary: A game can make a historical building instantly recognizable while changing its geometry and details. We compare architecture in Assassin’s Creed, Age of Empires, and Battlefield using global image similarity, local feature matching, a vision-language model, and human ratings. Their disagreements reveal how much an “accuracy” score depends on what is being measured.
question: Do computer-vision measures and human raters agree about the architectural fidelity of historical video games?
findings: In the matched main sample of 161 architectural objects, pooled standardized scores place Battlefield 0.778 units below Assassin’s Creed, while Age of Empires is close to Assassin’s Creed. These are observational comparisons of sampled depictions, not causal effects of game design.

The methods can reverse a franchise comparison: DINOv2 rates Age of Empires above Assassin’s Creed, whereas LightGlue rates it below. Global resemblance and local geometric correspondence capture different aspects of an architectural depiction.

Gemma aligns most closely with overall human ratings (r = 0.659) in 100 image comparisons rated by four people. The automated measures are only modestly aligned with one another, and LightGlue is especially sensitive to the reference photograph.

Architectural fidelity is one part of historical representation. Neither photographic resemblance nor agreement with these raters establishes historical accuracy in a game’s narrative, society, or culture.
sourceBasis: Complete 59-page public SSRN PDF (ssrn-6855021.pdf), dated 31 May 2026 on its title page, including sampling, model definitions, matched-sample models, human validation, robustness checks, discussion, and appendices. The downloaded archive retains 4,118 game images and 1,849 reference images across 110 locations; the shared main model sample is 161 objects / 483 model–object observations. Source pages use 1-based PDF pages. The original PDF exceeds the static host’s individual-file size limit; retain its authoritative SSRN full-text link.
limitations: The image archive is selective and does not cover entire game worlds; present-day reference photographs are imperfect evidence for a structure’s appearance in a historical period.
The main analysis uses the 161 objects shared by all three model outputs, rather than every retained image or every one of the 110 reference locations.

Four raters evaluate 100 image pairs; this is neither a representative player sample nor a validation by architectural historians. Gemma’s object-level multi-reference evaluations differ in unit from the pair-level image comparisons.

stories.title: Recognizable is not the same as geometrically faithful
stories.sourceBasis: Public SSRN 6855021 full text dated 31 May 2026; model-specific object-level regressions and visual-method definitions. These rankings concern the sampled architectural depictions, not the historical quality of entire franchises.
paragraphs: Which game franchise gets architecture right? The answer changes with the measuring instrument. In the main object-level comparisons, DINOv2’s broad visual resemblance places Age of Empires above Assassin’s Creed, while LightGlue’s local feature matching reverses that order. A recognizable silhouette can survive changes to proportions, materials, and details. We use that disagreement to make the meaning of an “accuracy” score visible.
limitations: The image archive is selective and does not cover entire game worlds; present-day reference photographs are imperfect evidence for a structure’s appearance in a historical period.

stories.title: An AI score still needs a human question
stories.sourceBasis: Public SSRN 6855021 full text; four-rater validation, correlations and limitations. Gemma uses object-level multi-reference evaluation; image-matching comparisons use pairs.
paragraphs: A vision-language model agrees more closely with our four raters’ overall impressions than the two image-matching methods do: Gemma’s correlation is 0.659 across 100 comparisons. That is useful evidence about perceived visual fidelity, but it does not make the model an architectural historian. A photograph of a building today, a player’s sense of plausibility, and evidence about its historical form answer related but different questions.
limitations: The image archive is selective and does not cover entire game worlds; present-day reference photographs are imperfect evidence for a structure’s appearance in a historical period.

title: Who’s Afraid of Coalition Talk? Mapping Polarization Among Northern Europe’s Cabinets in a Coevolving Latent Space
summary: Shared hashtags in 1,848,735 tweets are used to trace public communication among 518 cabinet ministers in seven Northern European democracies. Their topical ties persist over time, while the modeled dynamics of cross-bloc communication often diverge from the governing coalitions those countries sustain.
question: Do ministers’ public communication patterns reflect the coalitions they can form?
findings: The study follows cabinet ministers in Belgium, Denmark, Iceland, Ireland, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden from 2008 to 2024.
Year-to-year persistence is positive across all seven countries; within-party clustering is clearest in Ireland, Belgium and the Netherlands.

The center–right attraction estimate is negative in all seven countries, and the left–right estimate is negative except in Denmark, where it is approximately zero. These are modeled dynamics of topical overlap, not direct observations of personal hostility.
Sweden most closely matches a polarized bloc structure. In other countries, public discourse does not consistently mirror actual coalition arrangements.
sourceBasis: Complete 37-page SSRN manuscript downloaded through the normal SSRN browser flow on 23 November 2026 and reviewed, including yearly network construction, model interpretation, country results, discussion and appendix. Shared hashtags measure public topical overlap; they do not observe private bargaining, private beliefs, causal influence or coalition feasibility. The source uses a Cambridge manuscript template, which is not evidence of journal publication.

stories.title: Governing together does not mean talking alike
stories.summary: Cabinet ministers can sustain coalitions while keeping their public messages in separate ideological lanes. The paper finds that the political center rarely brings both sides together in this visible communication channel.
paragraphs: The study connects ministers when their hashtag use overlaps more than the country-year average, then models how those ties persist and change across ideological blocs. This makes the unit of analysis a recurring pattern of public attention rather than a direct conversation between two ministers.

Ireland provides an instructive mismatch: the clearest modeled cross-bloc coalescence is left–center, rather than the center–right pairing associated with its governing practice. Denmark’s center is internally coalescent without showing the same movement toward either flank.

Sweden is the clearest case in which the communication dynamics line up with a polarized bloc structure. Across the other cases, public talk is a limited guide to the private coordination that can make governing agreements possible.
limitations: Hashtag overlap is a measure of shared public topics; it does not necessarily mean agreement, friendship, hostility or direct interaction.
Only publicly available accounts and timelines can be observed; ministers without accounts and unavailable posts are missing.
Annual networks and long-window parameters emphasize durable patterns and can miss short-lived changes.
The paper does not observe private bargaining or establish causal effects of communication on coalition formation.

title: Kippas and Keffiyehs: Measuring Political Polarization in Israel through Interactions between Jewish and Arab Citizens
summary: Street-video images are used to estimate relative pedestrian distances and examine how spacing varies with visible identity cues. Pairs classified within the same ethnoreligious groups are generally closer in the modeled comparisons, while the method’s fine-grained labels and estimated depth introduce important measurement limits.
question: How do visible identity cues relate to interpersonal spacing in public?
findings: The public manuscript reports 449,992 detected pedestrians and 76,604 estimated pairwise distances from its street-video corpus.

In the gender-merged specifications, pairs classified as religious Arab are about 0.22–0.32 normalized distance units closer than the cross-group reference; the corresponding religious Jewish comparison is about 0.07–0.10 units. These are unitless within-frame comparisons, not meters.
The paper reports larger spacing for several pairings involving visible religious cues and for male-only pairs.
Detection performance depends strongly on label granularity: reported fine-grained mAP50 is about 0.19–0.21, increasing to about 0.56–0.58 when categories are aggregated.
sourceBasis: Complete 45-page public SSRN manuscript downloaded through the normal SSRN browser flow on 23 November 2026 and reviewed, including detection/depth validation, normalization, regressions and discussion. Author order follows this PDF’s title page, which differs from the landing-page order. Distances and visible identity labels are estimates/proxies, not direct readings of personal beliefs, calibrated physical meters, or causal evidence of avoidance. A later blinded local draft was compared but is not hosted and its additional electoral analyses are not transferred to this version.

stories.title: From a street scene to a relative distance
stories.summary: The method combines detected people, visible identity labels, and estimated depth. Its comparison is about relative spacing within a frame, which is a more limited claim than measuring people’s beliefs or intentions.
paragraphs: A street image is two-dimensional, so people who appear close in the picture may be at different depths. The study combines pedestrian detections with a monocular depth model, then normalizes pairwise distances within each frame so that comparisons use a unitless scale.

The central comparisons show closer estimated spacing for several same-group pairs relative to a cross-group reference. The source figure summarizes one of the gender-merged specifications: the red point is the reference intercept, while the other points are contrasts against it.

The classification task becomes harder as the labels become more detailed. Aggregating classes improves detection performance, illustrating a trade-off between identifying fine distinctions and measuring them reliably. Visible clothing and estimated spacing remain proxies, and they do not establish an individual’s private identity, political views or intent.
limitations: Monocular depth and within-frame normalization do not provide calibrated interpersonal distances in meters.
Visible religious or ethnonational categories are model/coder interpretations, rather than verified personal identities.
Fine-grained detection performance is substantially weaker than performance with aggregated categories; rare classes are especially difficult.
YouTube street-video coverage and a training sample centered on four cities constrain representativeness; the study is observational.

title: The Politics of Visibility: Party Symbols, Alliances, and Electoral Returns in Istanbul’s Mahalles
summary: Using 748,783 Google Street View panoramas of Istanbul, this study maps political and national symbols and connects their geography to official election returns. Denser party displays are associated with higher party vote shares but not greater turnout, while formal alliances leave little meaningful trace in the proximity of symbols.
question: How does parties’ street-level visual presence relate to electoral support, turnout, and the spatial organization of campaigning?
findings: An additional 10,000 detected party symbols is associated with 1.5–4.1 percentage points higher party vote share in models with party, date, and district fixed effects and socioeconomic controls.
Symbol counts have no statistically reliable association with turnout, and formal alliance membership does not meaningfully distinguish symbol proximity.
Major parties’ displays cluster tightly. These observational patterns do not establish that symbols cause electoral gains.
sourceBasis: Local 55-page author manuscript for SSRN 5369441; methods, results, discussion, and appendices reviewed. Vote-share models use 357 observations and turnout models 81. Roughly 1.22 million detections include national symbols as well as party symbols. Conflicting detector-accuracy and dispersion figures elsewhere in the draft are omitted.

title: HalalLLM vs. KosherLLM: When Abrahamic Scholars Confront Modern Questions through AI
summary: Three language models answer modern survey questions while prompted as twelve thinkers from Abrahamic traditions and supplied with retrieved texts. Aggregate means look similar, but median and modal response patterns differ across models, showing that a generated historical persona depends on the system used to construct it.
question: Does changing the language model change the historical thinker it appears to reconstruct?
findings: The design crosses twelve scholar personas, three language models, and 290 World Values Survey items, with five response rounds per model and scholar.
The reported repeated-measures tests find model differences in median and modal responses, while the mean comparison is not statistically significant.
Cross-religion aggregate comparisons have confidence intervals that include zero; the paper does not establish distinct, reliably separated religious value profiles.

These are generated survey profiles, not recovered historical answers. Numerical recoding, imputation, mixed item scales, and the small selected set of scholars limit interpretations of aggregate scores.
sourceBasis: Full SSRN manuscript downloaded through the ordinary authorized browser UI on 23 November 2026 and reviewed locally, including methods, results, discussion, and relevant appendices. 31-page manuscript. RAG and cleaning rules pp8–10; exploratory mapping pp10–11; statistical strategy pp12–15; discussion pp15–16; corpus and 290-item appendix pp18–28; response heatmaps pp29–31. The owner explicitly confirmed Ciarrah Wang as the correct coauthor name despite the downloaded cover reading Xinran Wang; retain the owner-confirmed spelling. No claim of historically authenticated beliefs or religious rankings is made.

stories.title: A historical thinker through three model voices
stories.sourceBasis: Full downloaded HalalLLM vs. KosherLLM manuscript: RAG/cleaning protocol, statistical results, discussion, and original response visualizations.
paragraphs: The same scholar and the same question can still lead to different generated answers. This study asks three language models to answer modern survey questions as twelve historical thinkers. Overall mean comparisons conceal differences that appear in median and modal responses. The maps and heatmaps help inspect that variation, while also showing why a convincing persona needs careful interpretation. The answers depend on model behavior, prompt design, retrieved material, and how missing or non-numeric replies are handled. They let researchers study representations of intellectual traditions; they do not establish what a historical person would actually have said.

title: SimCityNet: Quantifying Geo-Cultural Bias in AI-Generated Urban Videos through Interpretable Scene Embeddings
summary: SimCityNet uses interpretable scene measurements to compare Sora- and Kling-generated urban videos with Google Street View imagery from Europe and the Middle East. The study finds that fidelity varies by visual attribute and region, with compressed color variation rather than uniform homogenization of urban scenes.
question: How faithfully do text-to-video models portray urban environments across regions, and which visible attributes do they distort?
findings: The benchmark pairs 297,000 frames from 2,130 generated videos with 312,533 Street View photographs across 110 commercially active districts.
The aggregate tests do not support a general model advantage in its presumed familiar region; the clearest differences appear in particular visual attributes.
At the city level, color variance is approximately 45% of the Street View baseline for Sora and 13% for Kling, while vegetation, built surfaces, people, and vehicles do not show the same compression.
sourceBasis: Local 27-page author manuscript for SSRN 5369073; methods, results, conclusion, and geographic appendix reviewed. Findings concern the tested model versions and sampled commercial districts; uneven Street View coverage limits the benchmark.

title: DEVISE: Depth-Aware Vegetation Indexing System
summary: DEVISE measures street-level greenery by combining vegetation segmentation, color filtering, and estimated depth. Its application to an archive of 1.44 million panoramas explores the relationship between visible vegetation and electoral preferences in U.S. swing counties, with results interpreted as observational associations.
question: How should a nearby tree and distant greenery contribute to the same measurement?
findings: The pipeline separates trees, grass, and other plants, filters the masks using color information, and weights vegetation using estimated proximity to the viewer.
The application reports 1,441,746 panoramas collected for a 60-county swing-county sampling frame; actual coverage is uneven across counties and election-year months.

In the social-controls and fixed-effects models, recent Democratic vote share is positively associated with depth-adjusted grass and total greenery, while the tree-canopy coefficient is not statistically clear.
The regression tables use 174 county–date observations in the basic specification and 62 with social controls. These associations do not establish that voting patterns caused vegetation changes.
sourceBasis: Full SSRN manuscript downloaded through the ordinary authorized browser UI on 23 November 2026 and reviewed locally, including methods, results, discussion, and relevant appendices. 36-page manuscript dated 29 July 2025. Pipeline pp6–12, sampling and coverage pp13–17, model/results pp18–24 and Tables 2–4 pp22–23, appendix code pp27–36. Table 1 p15 shows uneven and empty cells, including no 2004 imagery. Abstract says 20-m spacing, while methods p13 say 50 m; no spacing claim is repeated on the site. Cover lists Junjie Zhao before Mingzhen Zhang.

stories.title: Measuring the greenery beside a pedestrian
stories.sourceBasis: Full downloaded DEVISE manuscript: pipeline, Figures 4 and 8, and model sample sizes/results in Tables 2–4.
paragraphs: A row of distant trees and a single tree over the sidewalk can occupy a similar number of green pixels while creating different street-level experiences. DEVISE combines segmentation, color checks, and depth estimates to give nearby vegetation more weight. The panorama pairs show which parts of a street survive those filters; the county maps show how the resulting measure differs from a plain pixel count. The large image archive supports an electoral application, but the final social-control models contain 62 county–date observations. Their associations with vote share are useful for generating questions about local environments, rather than proof that election results caused greener streets.

title: Fight or Flight on Fox?: Partisan Fear Responses on U.S. Cable News Shows
summary: Facial-expression estimates are linked to mentions of political actors in 1,750 cable-news videos. Mentions of the opposing party are associated with fear being the dominant estimated expression more often, with stronger and more precisely estimated patterns on Fox News than on MSNBC.
question: What changes in a listener’s expression when a political opponent is mentioned?
findings: The corpus contains 191 hours of video from CNN, MSNBC, and Fox News; the analysis focuses on non-speaking faces around timestamped political mentions.
Across the main specifications, fear is the top estimated expression about 7–10 percentage points more often around opposing-party mentions, against a 23.3% comparison mean.
Other emotion categories do not show the same consistent relationship; Fox News estimates are larger and more precise than MSNBC estimates.
The classifier achieved 66.37% accuracy on held-out FER2013 images. Human comparison rankings support its fear scores on a selected set of cable-news image pairs.
sourceBasis: Complete 38-page SSRN manuscript, dated 30 August 2022, downloaded through the normal SSRN browser flow on 23 November 2026 and reviewed, including methods, human validation, main tables and robustness appendices. This is observational evidence about estimated displayed expressions; it does not establish internal emotional states, causal reactions, or audience effects.

stories.title: Fear, rather than anger, is the most consistent signal
stories.summary: The study tests several estimated expressions around political mentions. Fear is the expression that most consistently separates opposing-party from other mentions.
paragraphs: A television discussion communicates through the people who are listening as well as the person speaking. This study extracts non-speaking faces, aligns them with timestamped mentions of political actors, and compares the estimated expressions across cable networks.

The clearest pattern is not increased anger or disgust. Fear is the dominant estimated expression about 7–10 percentage points more often around opposing-party mentions in the main specifications. The paper reports some evidence that the pattern is stronger on Fox News; MSNBC’s separate estimates are smaller and less precise.

The authors also ask human annotators to compare pairs of faces. Their rankings provide a check on the model’s relative fear scores, while leaving substantial limits on what a facial-expression measure can mean.
limitations: These are model estimates of displayed facial expressions, not direct readings of a person’s private feelings.
The videos are clips uploaded by networks to YouTube, and the channels’ collection windows differ.
The main regressions are observational and do not establish that a mention causes an expression or changes a viewer’s opinion.
Human validation uses a deliberately selected contrast between high- and low-classifier fear images; the principal plot restricts the sample to 668 pairs where two annotators agree.

title: The Imagined Congress: What Generative AI Models Think U.S. Politicians Look Like
summary: The study compares portraits from three image generators with verified characteristics of U.S. legislators, varying which information is included in each prompt. A common facial-analysis pipeline finds systematic differences even with full-information prompts, and masking changes those differences unevenly across demographic groups.
question: What do image generators assume about political representatives when a prompt leaves something out?
findings: The design compares DALL·E 3, Stable Diffusion and Adobe Firefly using full-information prompts and prompts that omit age, gender, race, ideology or legislative experience.
The generated portraits’ classifier-estimated ages are concentrated well below the legislators’ verified ages, including under the full-information prompt.

For legislators recorded as women, masking generally lowers the share of outputs classified as women relative to the full-information baseline; the corresponding shifts for legislators recorded as men are smaller.
The additional age shift under masking becomes more negative with longer legislative tenure, contrary to the paper’s initial “elder statesman” expectation.
Differences across platforms depend on the attribute and prompt condition; the platform comparison does not show that more safety curation uniformly produces more faithful portraits.
sourceBasis: Complete 100-page public SSRN manuscript downloaded through the ordinary SSRN browser flow and reviewed, including prompt design, feature extraction, three comparison designs, main findings, supplemental figures and all regression tables. No final journal publication is claimed. The large original remains in Downloads; authoritative SSRN links provide access. Findings describe classifier-estimated appearance in this research setup, not the subjects’ identities, voters’ reactions or a causal effect of a platform’s safety policy. Owner confirmed the CV working title is the same paper; current SSRN title and authors are used.

stories.title: Leaving out a detail is only part of the problem
stories.summary: The full-information portraits provide a crucial benchmark: some distortions appear before any attribute is removed.
paragraphs: The researchers build prompts from legislators’ public characteristics and then leave out one attribute at a time. The comparison gallery shows the resulting synthetic research images beside a real reference photograph. The generated outputs are test material, not authentic portraits of the person named in the figure.

The study separates two questions: how generated images differ from verified characteristics, and what changes when a detail is removed from the same person’s prompt. The age distributions illustrate why both comparisons matter. Generated faces are estimated as substantially younger even when all the specified information is supplied.

Masking also affects groups differently. The women-only analysis shows additional shifts toward man-coded outputs, while the comparable men-only shifts are smaller. The cross-platform plot makes another point: a platform’s curation label is not a reliable shortcut for how faithfully this particular task represents people.
limitations: Age, gender and race outputs come from a facial-analysis model; they are measurements of image appearance with their own possible errors, not verified personal identities.
Binary gender and White/non-White coding simplify multidimensional characteristics.
The platforms differ in training data, architecture, policies and generation settings, so their differences do not isolate a causal effect of safety curation.
The study does not test whether synthetic images change voter judgments or election outcomes.

title: Political Symbols and Urban Amenities: The Spatial Logic of Flag Placement in Istanbul
summary: Political and national symbols detected in Istanbul street imagery are linked with a geocoded database of urban amenities to study where campaign visibility concentrates. Symbols are more common in amenity-rich, commercially active settings, while evidence for party-specific sorting into expected amenity environments is limited.
question: How do urban amenities and electoral context relate to where parties display visible campaign symbols?
findings: The study combines 748,783 Street View panoramas with 75,984 unique amenities across Istanbul’s 39 districts and 1,009 precincts.
A one-standard-deviation increase in amenities within 250 meters is associated with 36.1% higher expected party-symbol counts.
High-exposure amenities have a stronger association with symbolic placement in competitive electoral settings; party-specific amenity sorting is limited after panorama fixed effects.
sourceBasis: Local 57-page author manuscript dated 6 May 2026, SSRN 6727981; data, methods, results, discussion, and robustness appendices reviewed. The estimates are observational associations, with limitations from uneven imagery coverage and automated measurement.
